claim: Extinction is not the erasure of the original learning but involves new learning that acts to suppress the original behaviour.
source: Current theories suggest extinction is not the erasure of the original learning but involves new learning that acts to suppress the original behaviour.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement presented in the abstract without specific data from this study, but is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The original behaviour can recover following the passage of time (spontaneous recovery).
source: Evidence for this can be found when the original behaviour recovers following the passage of time (spontaneous recovery) or reintroduction of the reinforcement (i.e. reinstatement).
evidence: This is established knowledge about extinction phenomena, referenced in the abstract.

claim: The original behaviour can recover following reintroduction of the reinforcement (reinstatement).
source: Evidence for this can be found when the original behaviour recovers following the passage of time (spontaneous recovery) or reintroduction of the reinforcement (i.e. reinstatement).
evidence: This is established knowledge about extinction phenomena, referenced in the abstract.

claim: Pharmacological manipulation of noradrenaline (NA) or its receptors can influence appetitive extinction.
source: Recent studies have shown that pharmacological manipulation of noradrenaline (NA) or its receptors can influence appetitive extinction; however, the role and source of endogenous NA in these effects are unknown.
evidence: This statement references recent studies and is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: The role and source of endogenous NA in appetitive extinction effects are unknown.
source: Recent studies have shown that pharmacological manipulation of noradrenaline (NA) or its receptors can influence appetitive extinction; however, the role and source of endogenous NA in these effects are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: LC stimulation during extinction trials did not change the rate of extinction.
source: LC stimulation during extinction trials did not change the rate of extinction but did serve to reduce subsequent spontaneous recovery, suggesting that stimulation of the LC can augment reward-related extinction.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: LC stimulation during extinction reduced subsequent spontaneous recovery.
source: LC stimulation during extinction trials did not change the rate of extinction but did serve to reduce subsequent spontaneous recovery, suggesting that stimulation of the LC can augment reward-related extinction.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Stimulation of the LC can augment reward-related extinction.
source: LC stimulation during extinction trials did not change the rate of extinction but did serve to reduce subsequent spontaneous recovery, suggesting that stimulation of the LC can augment reward-related extinction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings based on the observed reduction in spontaneous recovery.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of the LC during extinction trials reduced responding during the trials where it was applied.
source: Optogenetic inhibition of the LC during extinction trials reduced responding during the trials where it was applied, but no long-lasting changes in the retention of extinction were observed.
evidence: This is a finding from the inhibition experiment presented in Figure 4F.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of the LC during extinction trials produced no long-lasting changes in the retention of extinction.
source: Optogenetic inhibition of the LC during extinction trials reduced responding during the trials where it was applied, but no long-lasting changes in the retention of extinction were observed.
evidence: This is a finding from the inhibition experiment presented in Figure 4G.

claim: Not all LC cells expressed halorhodopsin in the inhibition experiment.
source: Since not all LC cells expressed halorhodopsin, it is possible that more complete LC inhibition or pathway-specific targeting would be more effective at suppressing extinction learning.
evidence: This is based on histological data showing 55% infection rate mentioned in the results.

claim: More complete LC inhibition or pathway-specific targeting might be more effective at suppressing extinction learning.
source: Since not all LC cells expressed halorhodopsin, it is possible that more complete LC inhibition or pathway-specific targeting would be more effective at suppressing extinction learning.
evidence: This is speculation based on the incomplete infection rate observed.

claim: Extinction involves new inhibitory learning, suppressing the original learned behaviour.
source: Contemporary theories of learning suggest that extinction is not simply the erasure of previous learning but rather involves new inhibitory learning, suppressing the original learned behaviour (Quirk and Mueller, 2008; Bouton et al., 2021; Iordanova et al., 2021; Bouton et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical work.

claim: Original learning can be uncovered following reintroduction of the original reinforcer (reinstatement).
source: Evidence for this comes from numerous demonstrations that the original learning can be uncovered following reintroduction of the original reinforcer (i.e. reinstatement; Rescorla and Heth, 1975), testing outside the extinction context (i.e. renewal; Bouton and King, 1983; García-Gutiérrez and Rosas, 2003; Nelson et al., 2011), or simply by allowing the passage of time between extinction training and testing (i.e. spontaneous recovery; Rescorla, 1996, Rescorla, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Original learning can be uncovered by testing outside the extinction context (renewal).
source: Evidence for this comes from numerous demonstrations that the original learning can be uncovered following reintroduction of the original reinforcer (i.e. reinstatement; Rescorla and Heth, 1975), testing outside the extinction context (i.e. renewal; Bouton and King, 1983; García-Gutiérrez and Rosas, 2003; Nelson et al., 2011), or simply by allowing the passage of time between extinction training and testing (i.e. spontaneous recovery; Rescorla, 1996, Rescorla, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Original learning can be uncovered by allowing the passage of time between extinction training and testing (spontaneous recovery).
source: Evidence for this comes from numerous demonstrations that the original learning can be uncovered following reintroduction of the original reinforcer (i.e. reinstatement; Rescorla and Heth, 1975), testing outside the extinction context (i.e. renewal; Bouton and King, 1983; García-Gutiérrez and Rosas, 2003; Nelson et al., 2011), or simply by allowing the passage of time between extinction training and testing (i.e. spontaneous recovery; Rescorla, 1996, Rescorla, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Blocking NA reuptake with atomoxetine can augment extinction of reward-related behaviours.
source: For example, blocking NA reuptake with atomoxetine can augment extinction of reward-related behaviours (Janak and Corbit, 2011; Janak et al., 2012; Furlong et al., 2015; Leung and Corbit, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The β-receptor antagonist propranolol impairs extinction learning related to rewarding events.
source: In contrast, the application of the β-receptor antagonist propranolol impairs extinction learning related to rewarding (Janak and Corbit, 2011; Janak et al., 2012; Leung and Corbit, 2017) and fear-provoking events (Berlau and McGaugh, 2006; Do-Monte et al., 2010; Mueller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The β-receptor antagonist propranolol impairs extinction learning related to fear-provoking events.
source: In contrast, the application of the β-receptor antagonist propranolol impairs extinction learning related to rewarding (Janak and Corbit, 2011; Janak et al., 2012; Leung and Corbit, 2017) and fear-provoking events (Berlau and McGaugh, 2006; Do-Monte et al., 2010; Mueller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: A surge in NA release coincides with the omission of an expected reward.
source: Consistent with a role in extinction, experiments using fast-scan voltammetry observed a surge in NA release that coincided with the omission of an expected reward implicating the endogenous noradrenergic system in detecting extinction contingencies (Park et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an empirical study using voltammetry.

claim: The LC has direct anatomical connections with the basolateral amygdala (BLA).
source: It is likely that projections originating in the locus coeruleus (LC) are responsible as the LC has direct anatomical connections with multiple brain regions that contribute to extinction, including the basolateral amygdala (BLA) and the infralimbic cortex (IFC) (McCall et al., 2017; Uematsu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The LC has direct anatomical connections with the infralimbic cortex (IFC).
source: It is likely that projections originating in the locus coeruleus (LC) are responsible as the LC has direct anatomical connections with multiple brain regions that contribute to extinction, including the basolateral amygdala (BLA) and the infralimbic cortex (IFC) (McCall et al., 2017; Uematsu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: LC activity increased when rats were presented with novel stimuli.
source: Previous studies that recorded LC activity in freely behaving rats observed that LC activity increased when rats were presented with novel stimuli, and while this response rapidly habituated, LC activity rapidly increased again when a stimulus was followed by reward (Sara et al., 1994), suggesting that the LC responds to novelty.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an electrophysiological recording study.

claim: LC activity rapidly increased when a stimulus was followed by reward.
source: Previous studies that recorded LC activity in freely behaving rats observed that LC activity increased when rats were presented with novel stimuli, and while this response rapidly habituated, LC activity rapidly increased again when a stimulus was followed by reward (Sara et al., 1994), suggesting that the LC responds to novelty.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an electrophysiological recording study.

claim: The LC response to novel stimuli rapidly habituated.
source: Previous studies that recorded LC activity in freely behaving rats observed that LC activity increased when rats were presented with novel stimuli, and while this response rapidly habituated, LC activity rapidly increased again when a stimulus was followed by reward (Sara et al., 1994), suggesting that the LC responds to novelty.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an electrophysiological recording study.

claim: The LC increased activity when stimulus-reinforcer contingencies were reversed.
source: However, the LC was also reported to increase activity when stimulus-reinforcer contingencies were reversed and during extinction (Sara and Segal, 1991; Sara et al., 1994; Bouret and Sara, 2004), suggesting that the LC may not simply be responding to novelty, but also to changes in expected outcomes in order to facilitate a corresponding change in behaviour.
evidence: This is supported by citations to electrophysiological recording studies.

claim: The LC increased activity during extinction.
source: However, the LC was also reported to increase activity when stimulus-reinforcer contingencies were reversed and during extinction (Sara and Segal, 1991; Sara et al., 1994; Bouret and Sara, 2004), suggesting that the LC may not simply be responding to novelty, but also to changes in expected outcomes in order to facilitate a corresponding change in behaviour.
evidence: This is supported by citations to electrophysiological recording studies.

claim: Lesions of the LC impaired extinction of conditioned fear.
source: Looking back to earlier studies that directly tied LC manipulations to extinction learning, lesions of the LC were shown to impair extinction of conditioned fear (Mason and Fibiger, 1978) and 6-OHDA lesions targeting the dorsal noradrenergic bundle slowed extinction in an appetitive runway task (Mason and Iversen, 1975), although electrolytic lesions of the LC, which deplete forebrain NA less completely, were found to have little impact on appetitive extinction (Koob et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a lesion study.

claim: 6-OHDA lesions targeting the dorsal noradrenergic bundle slowed extinction in an appetitive runway task.
source: Looking back to earlier studies that directly tied LC manipulations to extinction learning, lesions of the LC were shown to impair extinction of conditioned fear (Mason and Fibiger, 1978) and 6-OHDA lesions targeting the dorsal noradrenergic bundle slowed extinction in an appetitive runway task (Mason and Iversen, 1975), although electrolytic lesions of the LC, which deplete forebrain NA less completely, were found to have little impact on appetitive extinction (Koob et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a lesion study.

claim: Electrolytic lesions of the LC had little impact on appetitive extinction.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to a lesion study.

claim: Electrolytic lesions of the LC deplete forebrain NA less completely than other lesion methods.
source: Looking back to earlier studies that directly tied LC manipulations to extinction learning, lesions of the LC were shown to impair extinction of conditioned fear (Mason and Fibiger, 1978) and 6-OHDA lesions targeting the dorsal noradrenergic bundle slowed extinction in an appetitive runway task (Mason and Iversen, 1975), although electrolytic lesions of the LC, which deplete forebrain NA less completely, were found to have little impact on appetitive extinction (Koob et al., 1978).
evidence: This is established knowledge about different lesion methods.

claim: Recent studies using optogenetic or chemogenetic methods to activate the LC have reported conflicting results on extinction.
source: While more recent studies using either optogenetic or chemogenetic methods to activate the LC have reported somewhat conflicting results, in some cases enhancing and other cases disrupting extinction (Uematsu et al., 2017; Giustino et al., 2019; Giustino et al., 2020), this could be explained by the differences in levels of fear, differences in the intensity of stimulation, as strong LC stimulation can be fear promoting, or by an increasing appreciation of the modular organization of the LC and differential role of different projection targets (Uematsu et al., 2017; Chandler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent optogenetic and chemogenetic studies.

claim: Strong LC stimulation can be fear promoting.
source: While more recent studies using either optogenetic or chemogenetic methods to activate the LC have reported somewhat conflicting results, in some cases enhancing and other cases disrupting extinction (Uematsu et al., 2017; Giustino et al., 2019; Giustino et al., 2020), this could be explained by the differences in levels of fear, differences in the intensity of stimulation, as strong LC stimulation can be fear promoting, or by an increasing appreciation of the modular organization of the LC and differential role of different projection targets (Uematsu et al., 2017; Chandler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Recent studies have largely focused on the extinction of conditioned fear.
source: It is important to note that recent studies have largely focused on the extinction of conditioned fear and relatively less is known about whether LC stimulation can modulate extinction of reward-related behaviours.
evidence: This is an observation about the state of the literature.

claim: Fear conditioning paradigms inherently involve noxious stimulation.
source: This distinction is not trivial because fear conditioning paradigms also inherently involve noxious stimulation, the impact of which can be amplified by LC stimulation, and these paradigms involve a degree of stress or anxiety, conditions tied to NA levels (e.g. Chiang and Aston-Jones, 1993; Giustino et al., 2019; Uematsu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about fear conditioning paradigms.

source: While electrophysiological recording data show that LC neurons respond to sudden reward omission (Sara and Segal, 1991; Sara et al., 1994; Su and Cohen, 2022), these results have been inconsistent (Bouret and Sara, 2004).

claim: 43 male and female rats were randomly divided into three treatment groups in the first experiment.
source: In the first experiment, 43 male and female rats were randomly divided into three treatment groups: A channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) group, which consisted of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-Cre rats injected with AAV5-EF1a-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-mCherry, an offset group, which consisted of TH-Cre rats injected with the same virus expressing ChR2 but received stimulation during the inter-trial intervals (ITI), and controls, which consisted of TH-Cre Long–Evans (LE) rats (n = 7, receiving light pulses during the CS) and wild-type LE rats (receiving light pulses during CS presentations; n = 8, or during the ITI; n = 7) injected with the control virus (AAV5-EF1a-DIO-mCherry).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and groups.

claim: There were no differences between TH-Cre and wild-type controls during training.
source: Preliminary analyses demonstrated no differences between TH-Cre and wild-type controls (stimulus and offset) during training [Figure 1E; F(2,19) = 1.149, p=0.338], extinction [Figure 1F; F(2,19) = 1.883, p=0.179], or testing [Figure 1G; test 1: F(2,19) = 0.352, p=0.708; test 2: F(2,19) = 0.250, p=0.781], and so they were collapsed for further analyses and are henceforth referred to as the control group.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There were no differences between TH-Cre and wild-type controls during extinction.

evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1G.

evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Lever-pressing rates decreased across days of extinction.

evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was an effect of group in the first spontaneous recovery test.
source: In this test, there was an effect of group [test 1; Figure 2D; F(2, 40) = 4.037, p=0.025] and pairwise comparisons demonstrated that rats in the ChR2 group responded significantly less compared to control [t(35) = 2.9.04, p=0.003] or offset [t(19) = 1.735, p=0.049] groups.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2D.

source: When manipulated during extinction rather than fear conditioning, optogenetic inhibition of IFC-projecting LC neurons impaired learning, whereas inhibition of BLA-projecting neurons during extinction enhanced expression of extinction learning 24 hr later (Uematsu et al., 2017), suggesting that LC efferents modulate fear and extinction in a pathway-specific manner.

claim: LC efferents modulate fear and extinction in a pathway-specific manner.

claim: The time period in which NA exerts its effect is critical for learning.
